abstract: Mutations in the BSN gene, encoding the presynaptic protein Bassoon, are implicated in epilepsy, but their impact on astrocytes remains unclear. Using CRISPR/Cas9, we introduced patient-derived BSN mutations (p.M1903V and c.5672insCG) into human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and differentiated them into astrocytes. We found that mutant astrocytes exhibited significant lipid accumulation, evidenced by elevated free cholesterol, reduced arginase activity, and increased lipid droplets. Proteomic analysis revealed upregulation of lipid metabolism regulators, such as APOE and FASN. Electrophysiological recordings showed impaired Kir4.1 potassium channel function, depolarized resting membrane potential, and increased capacitance in mutant astrocytes following kainic acid stimulation. Co-culture experiments with neurons demonstrated that BSN-mutant astrocytes led to reduced neurite outgrowth, elevated neuronal apoptosis, increased pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α), and neuronal hyperexcitability. These findings demonstrate that BSN mutations disrupt astrocyte lipid homeostasis and impair neurosupportive functions, thereby driving neuronal hyperexcitability. This study establishes astrocytes as critical mediators of epilepsy pathogenesis in BSN-related disorders and highlights lipid metabolism as a potential therapeutic target.

Materials and Methods
Cell culture and maintenance
iPSC Culture: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) (iPSN0077 Passage 30) were obtained from commercial vendors, and maintained in mTeSR1 medium (#85850, Stemcell Technologies, Canada) on Matrigel-coated plates (#354277, Corning®, USA). Cells were passaged using Accutase (#AT104, Innovative Cell Technologies, USA) every 5–7 days at a split ratio of 1:6 to 1:10 and cultured at 37 ​°C in a humidified atmosphere with 5 ​% CO
2
.
Neural Stem Cell (NSC) Culture: iPSCs were differentiated into NSCs as previously described [
36
]. In brief, neural induction medium (DMEM/F12 supplemented with N2, B27, EGF, and FGF) was used. NSCs were cultured as monolayers or neurospheres.
Astrocyte Culture: NSCs were further differentiated into astrocytes as previously described [
37
]. In brief, using astrocyte differentiation medium (DMEM/F12 supplemented with FBS, CNTF, and BMP4). Astrocytes were maintained until they expressed mature markers (GFAP, ALDH1L1, S100B).
Neuronal Culture: NSCs were differentiated into neurons as previously described [
38
]. In brief, neuronal induction medium (Neurobasal medium supplemented with B27, BDNF, GDNF, and cAMP) was used. Neuronal differentiation was confirmed by immunostaining for MAP2 and NeuN.
CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing
Design of gRNAs: Single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) targeting the
BSN
gene (p.M1903V, c.5707A ​> ​G) were designed using an online tool (CRISPOR,
http://crispor.tefor.net/and
). sgRNAs were cloned into the pSpCas9(BB)-2A-Puro vector. All primers used are listed in
Supplementary Table 1
.
Transfection and Selection: iPSCs were transfected with CRISPR/Cas9 constructs using Lipofectamine Stem Transfection Reagent. Transfected cells were selected with puromycin, and single-cell clones were expanded.
Genotyping: Genomic DNA was extracted from clones, and the targeted regions were amplified by PCR. Sanger sequencing was performed to confirm the introduction of mutations.
All edited clones underwent rigorous quality control: Karyotyping confirmed normal chromosomal integrity (46, XX;
Supplementary Fig. 2
); Potential off-target sites (top 5 predicted by CRISPOR) were analyzed by Sanger sequencing, confirming no unintended indels (
Supplementary Table 3
and
Fig. 3
). This ensures observed phenotypes are BSN mutation-specific rather than technical artifacts.
Exosome isolation and characterization
Exosome Isolation: Exosomes were isolated from NSC-conditioned medium using differential ultracentrifugation (300×
g
for 10 ​min, 10,000×
g
for 30 ​min, and 100,000×
g
for 70 ​min). The pellet was resuspended in PBS.
Western Blotting: Exosome markers (Hsp70, CD63, TSG101) were detected by Western blotting using specific antibodies (all antibodies used in this study are listed in
Supplementary Table 2
).
Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM): Exosome morphology was analyzed by TEM after negative staining with uranyl acetate.
Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis (NTA): Exosome size and concentration were measured using a NanoSight NS300 instrument.
Proteomic analysis
Protein Extraction: Proteins were extracted from NSCs using RIPA buffer supplemented with protease inhibitors. Protein concentration was quantified using a BCA assay.
Mass Spectrometry: Proteins were digested with trypsin, and peptides were analyzed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) on a Q Exactive HF-X mass spectrometer.
Data Analysis: Raw data were processed using MaxQuant software, and differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were identified. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analyses were performed using DAVID and Metascape, including all DEPs with FDR <0.05, regardless of expression direction. Protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks were performed using STRING and Cytoscape.
Electrophysiological recordings
Patch-Clamp Setup: Astrocytes were plated on glass coverslips, and whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were performed using a Multiclamp 700B amplifier. Data were acquired using pCLAMP software.
Resting Membrane Potential (RMP): RMP was measured in current-clamp mode (I ​= ​0).
Kir4.1 Current Density: Voltage-clamp recordings were performed to measure Kir4.1 currents in response to voltage steps (−150 ​mV to +50 ​mV). Current density was calculated by normalizing currents to cell capacitance.
Kainic Acid (KA) Stimulation: Astrocytes were treated with KA (100 ​μM) for 10 ​min before recordings to induce hyperexcitability.
Lipid metabolism assays
Oil Red O Staining: Astrocytes were fixed with 4 ​% paraformaldehyde and stained with Oil Red O to visualize lipid droplets. Staining was quantified using ImageJ.
Free Cholesterol Measurement: Free cholesterol levels were measured using a fluorometric assay kit (Abcam). Fluorescence was read using a microplate reader.
Arginase Activity Assay: Arginase activity was measured using a colorimetric assay kit (Sigma-Aldrich). Absorbance was read at 450 ​nm.
Immunostaining and imaging
Immunofluorescence: Cells were fixed with 4 ​% paraformaldehyde, permeabilized with 0.1 ​% Triton X-100, and blocked with 5 ​% BSA. Primary antibodies were incubated overnight, followed by secondary antibodies conjugated to fluorophores. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (all antibodies used in this study are listed in
Supplementary Table 2
).
Confocal Microscopy: Images were acquired using a Zeiss LSM 880 confocal microscope and analyzed using ZEN software.
Co-culture experiments
Astrocyte-Neuron Co-Culture: Astrocytes were co-cultured with neurons in a transwell system or direct contact system. Neuronal activity was assessed by immunostaining for activity markers (C-fos, Zif268, Arc).
Neurite Outgrowth Assay: Neurons were stained with β–III–tubulin, and neurite length was quantified using ImageJ.
Apoptosis and inflammation assays
Flow Cytometry: Neurons were stained with Annexin V and propidium iodide (PI) to assess apoptosis. Data were acquired using a BD FACSCanto II flow cytometer and analyzed with FlowJo software (all antibodies used in this study are listed in
Supplementary Table 2
).
Western Blotting: Apoptotic markers (Bcl-2, Bax, BKCa, Cleaved Caspase-3) were detected by Western blotting (all antibodies used in this study are listed in
Supplementary Table 2
).
Cytokine Measurement: Levels of inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) in co-culture supernatants were measured using ELISA kits (R&D Systems).
ROS Measurement: Intracellular ROS levels were measured using a DCFDA assay. Fluorescence was read using a microplate reader.
Statistical analysis
Data Analysis: GraphPad Prism 10.1.2 or R Program (version 4.3.2) was used for all statistical analyses. Unpaired
t
-test or one-way ANOVA were used to determine statistical significance, followed by Dunnett's test for multiple comparisons. All quantitative data are presented as mean ​± ​SD. Statistical significance was considered as ∗p ​< ​0.05, ∗∗p ​< ​0.01, ∗∗∗p ​< ​0.001.

Co-culture experiments
Astrocyte-Neuron Co-Culture: Astrocytes were co-cultured with neurons in a transwell system or direct contact system. Neuronal activity was assessed by immunostaining for activity markers (C-fos, Zif268, Arc).
Neurite Outgrowth Assay: Neurons were stained with β–III–tubulin, and neurite length was quantified using ImageJ.

Introduction
Epilepsy, a debilitating neurological disorder affecting 50 million people globally, is characterized by recurrent seizures and imposes substantial social and personal burdens [
[1]
,
[2]
,
[3]
]. Its pathogenesis involves a complex interplay of genetic predispositions, structural brain abnormalities, metabolic disturbances, infections, and immune responses [
4
,
5
]. Recent advances in genetic research have identified numerous mutations associated with epilepsy, underscoring the critical role of genetic factors in its development [
[6]
,
[7]
,
[8]
,
[9]
]. Among these mutations, the
BSN
gene, which encodes the bassoon protein, has emerged as a significant focus of interest [
10
]. Bassoon serves as a crucial scaffolding protein that organizes the presynaptic cytoskeleton at the active zone (CAZ), where neurotransmitter release takes place [
11
]. Mutations in the
BSN
gene have been implicated in epilepsy, indicating that disruptions in synaptic function and the remodeling of the extracellular matrix in nerve cells may contribute to the disease's pathogenesis [
12
,
13
]. However, the specific mechanisms by which
BSN
mutations lead to epilepsy remain poorly understood, particularly regarding their downstream effects on non-neuronal cells, such as astrocytes.
Pathogenic BSN variants have been shown to impair human neuronal function in a cell-autonomous manner [
14
]. For example, missense mutations (e.g., p.Arg1066Cys) disrupt synaptic vesicle reloading and attenuate high-frequency neurotransmission [
15
,
16
]. C-terminal variants such as p.Pro3866Ala promote protein aggregation and tau pathology, compromising presynaptic function [
17
,
18
]. Moreover, defective proteostasis via impaired interactions with Siah1 and Atg5 has been linked to synaptic degeneration [
19
,
20
].
While BSN is classically regarded as a neuron-enriched presynaptic scaffold, recent single-cell transcriptomic datasets reveal its detectable expression in astrocytes across species (human arcuate nucleus:
GSE255968
; mouse cortex:
GSE280481
). The comparable expression levels between astrocytes and neurons in these datasets suggest potential non-neuronal functions for BSN, warranting investigation of its role in astrocyte physiology and pathology.
Astrocytes, the most abundant glial cells in the central nervous system, play a crucial role in maintaining brain homeostasis and regulating neuronal activity [
[21]
,
[22]
,
[23]
]. Recent studies have underscored the critical role of astrocytes in epilepsy, with increasing evidence indicating that dysregulation of lipid metabolism within these cells may play a significant role in the development and progression of the disease [
24
,
25
]. Lipids play a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of cell membranes, facilitating signal transduction, and supporting energy metabolism within the brain [
26
]. Dysregulated lipid metabolism in astrocytes can impair neuronal-glial interactions, modify synaptic transmission, and induce hyperexcitability, ultimately resulting in seizures [
[27]
,
[28]
,
[29]
]. Despite these insights, the specific mechanisms linking astrocytic lipid accumulation to epilepsy, particularly in the context of genetic mutations such as those in the
BSN
gene, remain largely unexplored.
Recent progress in the field of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and genome editing has provided powerful tools for modeling epilepsy and investigating its genetic basis. Human iPSCs, derived from patient somatic cells through reprogramming, can be differentiated into various neuronal and glial cell types, including astrocytes, and have emerged as a valuable platform for studying the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying epilepsy [
30
,
31
]. The integration of CRISPR/Cas9 technology further enhances the utility of iPSCs by enabling precise genetic modifications, allowing researchers to introduce or correct specific mutations in a controlled genetic background [
32
,
33
]. This approach has been successfully applied to model various epilepsy-associated mutations, providing insights into disease mechanisms and potential therapeutic targets [
34
,
35
].
In this study, our objective is to investigate the effects of specific mutations in the
BSN
gene (p.M1903V, c.5707A ​> ​G, and c.5672insCG) on epilepsy. The mutation BSN c.5707 (exon5) A ​> ​G leading to the M1903V de novo mutation, was initially identified in a young patient with epilepsy. We constructed both heterozygous (BSN
M1903V/wt
) and homozygous (BSN
M1903V/M1903V
) mutations, and notably an additional frameshift mutation, c.5672insCG (BSN
5672insCG/wt
), was generated. This serendipitous discovery provided a unique opportunity to explore the consequences of these mutations. We aimed to determine what would occur in the presence of the homozygous mutation and whether the frameshift mutation could induce epilepsy. If so, it would strongly suggest that loss-of-function mutations in BSN are the primary cause of the disease. To explore their functional consequences, we utilized CRISPR/Cas9 technology to introduce these mutations into human iPSCs. We hypothesize that mutations in the
BSN
gene lead to dysregulation of lipid metabolism in astrocytes, which subsequently disrupts neuronal function and contributes to the process of epileptogenesis. To test this hypothesis, we generated BSN-mutant neural stem cells (NSCs) derived from CRISPR/Cas9 edited h-iPSCs, and performed a proteomic analysis to identify differentially expressed proteins, with a particular emphasis on lipid metabolism pathways. Furthermore, we differentiated these NSCs into astrocytes and assessed their functional impact on neuronal cells.
Our results reveal that BSN mutations promote lipid accumulation in astrocytes, resulting in hyperexcitability, impaired Kir4.1 channel function, and subsequent neuronal dysfunction. These findings establish a mechanistic link between BSN mutations and epileptogenesis, underscoring the critical role of lipid homeostasis in preserving astrocyte-neuron interactions. By elucidating the downstream effects of BSN mutations on astrocyte function and lipid metabolism, this study uncovers novel mechanisms underlying epilepsy and identifies potential therapeutic targets. Utilizing h-iPSCs and advanced proteomics, our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the role of BSN mutations in epilepsy and lays the groundwork for future investigations into lipid dysregulation as a critical driver of neurological disorders.

Results
Generation and validation of BSN-mutant iPSCs
Using CRISPR/Cas9 technology, we successfully introduced BSN mutations (BSN
5672insCG/wt
, BSN
M1903V/wt
, and BSN
M1903V/M1903V
) into a healthy human iPSC line, and used BSN
wt/wt
as control.
Fig. 1
A illustrates the schematic diagram of the construction of the three clones and their validation through Sanger sequencing. The BSN mutant iPSCs exhibited typical embryonic stem cell morphology (
Fig. 1
B). The results of the immunofluorescence analysis for pluripotency markers (NANOG, OCT4, SSEA-4, TRA-1-60) confirmed that the cells remained in an undifferentiated state (
Supplementary Fig. 1
). Embryoid body (EB) formation assays demonstrated that the mutant iPSCs retained the ability to differentiate into mesoderm (CTNT), endoderm (AFP), and ectoderm (SOX1) lineages, indicating that the BSN mutations did not compromise their pluripotency or differentiation potential (
Fig. 1
C).
Fig. 1
Generation and characterization of BSN-mutant iPSCs. (A) Schematic of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated introduction of BSN mutations (BSN
5672insCG/wt
, BSN
M1903V/wt
, BSN
M1903V/M1903V
) and Sanger sequencing validation. (B) Morphology of BSN-mutant iPSCs resembling human embryonic stem cells. Scale bar: 200 ​μm. (C) Embryoid body (EB) differentiation assay showing trilineage potential (endoderm: AFP; mesoderm: CTNT; ectoderm: SOX1; DAPI, blue). Scale bar: 50 ​μm.
Fig. 1
To confirm the genomic fidelity of edited lines, we performed: Karyotype analysis revealing normal 46, XX chromosomal composition across all mutants (
Supplementary Fig. 2
); Interrogation of top 5 potential off-target sites (predicted by CRISPOR) via Sanger sequencing, which showed no indels (
Supplementary Fig. 3A–E
; sequences in
Supplementary Table 3
). These data verify that the observed phenotypes are attributable to targeted BSN mutations rather than off-target effects or chromosomal instability.
Critically, despite sharing an identical genetic background, the three mutant genotypes exhibited distinct severity gradients (BSN
5672insCG/wt
, BSN
M1903V/wt
, and BSN
M1903V/M1903V
) across lipid accumulation (
Fig. 4
), electrophysiological deficits (
Fig. 5
), and neuronal toxicity (
Fig. 7
,
Fig. 8
). This genotype-phenotype correlation within an isogenic system provides compelling evidence for BSN-specific causality, excluding clonal variation confounders.
Differentiation of BSN-mutant iPSCs into neural stem cells (NSCs)
The BSN-mutant iPSCs were efficiently differentiated into neural stem cells (NSCs), as evidenced by the expression of NSC markers SOX1 and Nestin (
Fig. 2
A). Given Bassoon's role in presynaptic vesicle cycling and emerging evidence that neuronal precursors secrete exosomes carrying synaptic regulators [
39
,
40
], we asked whether BSN mutations alter the proteomic cargo of NSC-derived exosomes. These vesicles may reflect early disruptions in synaptic protein trafficking prior to neuronal maturation. Western blotting confirmed the presence of exosome-specific markers (Hsp70, CD63, TSG101), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) revealed no significant differences in exosome morphology, size, or internalization capacity between mutant and control NSCs (
Fig. 2
B–D). However, CCK-8 assays revealed that BSN
M1903V/M1903V
and BSN
5672insCG/wt
NSCs exhibited reduced proliferation compared to controls, as cell viability dropped to 42 ​% and 65 ​% respectively (p ​< ​0.01), while BSN
M1903V/wt
NSCs showed no significant difference (
Fig. 2
E).

Proteomic analysis reveals dysregulated lipid metabolism in BSN-mutant NSCs
To further elucidate the underlying mechanism that BSN mutation may affect, proteomic analysis was performed in NSCs. 8719 proteins were identified in all groups, with significant differential expression in BSN-mutant NSCs compared to controls (
Fig. 3
A and B). As shown in
Fig. 3
B, DEPs comprised both upregulated and downregulated proteins. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses (
Fig. 3
C) were performed using all significant DEPs (both up- and down-regulated), revealing bidirectional disruptions pathways related to lipid metabolism, membrane transport, and endocrine metabolism (
Fig. 3
C). Protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks showed interplay with lipid metabolism-related proteins (e.g. APOE, APOB, FASN) were identified among BSN mutant and normal NSCs (
Fig. 3
D). RT-qPCR and western blotting analysis confirmed upregulation of APOE, APOB, FASN in BSN-mutant NSCs, with the highest expression observed in BSN
5672insCG/wt
, followed by BSN
M1903V/M1903V
and BSN
M1903V/wt
(
Fig. 3
E and F). These findings suggest that BSN mutations may disrupt lipid metabolism in NSCs.
Lipid accumulation and metabolic dysregulation in BSN-mutant astrocytes
Proteomic profiling of BSN-mutant NSCs revealed significant upregulation of lipid metabolism regulators (APOE, APOB, FASN;
Fig. 3
E and F), suggesting a cell-intrinsic disruption of lipid homeostasis. Since astrocytes are the primary lipid-metabolizing cells in the CNS and show heightened susceptibility to metabolic disturbances during neural differentiation [
41
], we next asked whether these lipid-handling defects would manifest functionally upon differentiation into astrocytes. Specifically, we hypothesized that the lipid dysregulation observed in undifferentiated NSCs would amplify during astrocyte maturation given their specialized role in lipid storage and transport [
42
], and would be exacerbated under excitatory conditions that mimic epileptiform activity.
Bioinformatic analysis of public single-cell transcriptomic datasets confirmed BSN expression in astrocytes. In
GSE255968
(human arcuate nucleus), BSN transcripts were detected in astrocyte clusters. In
GSE280481
(mouse cortex, normal sleep condition), BSN expression levels in astrocytes (mean 4.72) were comparable to neurons (mean 5.75), suggesting that BSN may exert functions in both glial and neuronal contexts (
Supplementary Fig. 4
).
To test this, we differentiated BSN-mutant NSCs into astrocytes and assessed lipid homeostasis following kainic acid challenge. Astrocyte markers (GFAP, ALDH1L1, S100B) were confirmed by immunofluorescence (
Fig. 4
A). Western blotting confirmed the loss of BSN expression (at 416kD) in mutant astrocytes (
Fig. 4
B). KA stimulation induced significant lipid accumulation in BSN-mutant astrocytes, as evidenced by increased free cholesterol levels and reduced arginase activity (
Fig. 4
C and D). Levels of cholesterol were increased after KA stimulation, and higher levels were observed in BSN-mutant astrocytes compared to BSN
wt/wt
astrocytes (BSN
5672insCG/wt

Discussion
This study demonstrates that loss-of-function mutations in the
BSN
gene (p.M1903V and c.5672insCG) promote lipid accumulation in human astrocytes, leading to hyperexcitability, impaired Kir4.1 channel function, and neuronal dysfunction. Using CRISPR/Cas9-generated BSN-mutant iPSCs, we observed that these mutations disrupt lipid metabolism pathways, as evidenced by the upregulation of lipid-related proteins (APOE, APOB, FASN) and increased lipid droplet accumulation in astrocytes. Furthermore, BSN-mutant astrocytes exhibited significant electrophysiological abnormalities, including depolarized resting membrane potential, reduced Kir4.1 current density, and increased cell capacitance upon kainic acid (KA) stimulation. These changes were associated with neuronal hyperexcitability, inflammation, and apoptosis, suggesting a direct link between BSN mutations, astrocyte dysfunction, and epileptogenesis.
Although BSN is classically characterized as a presynaptic scaffolding protein, recent studies show that astrocytes can express a broad repertoire of synaptic proteins, including scaffolding molecules traditionally considered neuron-specific [
[45]
,
[46]
,
[47]
]. Such non-neuronal expression patterns suggest potential roles for BSN in astrocyte-mediated synaptic modulation, metabolic support, and activity-dependent structural plasticity. Our study is the first, to our knowledge, to explore BSN function in astrocytes. Transcriptomic data from both human and mouse brain show astrocytic BSN expression, supporting our experimental rationale. Given astrocytes’ roles in synaptic regulation, metabolism, and lipid handling, BSN mutations may disrupt these processes in a manner that complements or amplifies neuronal dysfunction.
While the cell-autonomous neuronal effects of BSN mutations are well documented [
14
], our findings highlight a complementary, glial dimension of pathology. By uncovering persistent cholesterol accumulation and impaired metabolic responses in BSN-mutant astrocytes, we expand the spectrum of BSN-related mechanisms beyond presynaptic dysfunction, suggesting that both neuronal and astroglial compartments jointly drive disease progression.
While exosomes are not direct proxies for synaptic vesicles, their proteomic profile can reveal alterations in presynaptic machinery. For example, exosomes from neural cells carry synaptic proteins and are implicated in modulating neuronal excitability [
48
]. Our observation of unchanged exosome biogenesis in BSN-mutant NSCs (
Fig. 2
B–D) suggests that initial vesicle secretion mechanisms remain intact, though cargo-specific defects may emerge upon neuronal differentiation—a hypothesis warranting future investigation.
The
BSN
-encoded bassoon protein is a cornerstone of presynaptic active zone (CAZ) organization, where it orchestrates synaptic vesicle clustering, Ca
2+
channel positioning, and neurotransmitter release [
11
,
49
]. Our identified mutations (p.M1903V, c.5707A ​> ​G, c.5672insCG) likely impair these functions through distinct mechanisms. The p.M1903V variant, located in the coiled-coil domain, may destabilize Bassoon-Piccolo interactions, compromising CAZ assembly and vesicle docking [
50
,
51
]. This aligns with studies showing that Bassoon-deficient synapses exhibit asynchronous neurotransmitter release and reduced synaptic fidelity, predisposing neuronal networks to hypersynchronization [
52
]. Similarly, the c.5672insCG mutation, which disrupts mRNA stability, could diminish Bassoon expression, impairing the transport of CAZ precursors from the Golgi apparatus [
53
,
54
]. Such structural deficits may explain the observed synaptic vesicle asynchrony and hyperexcitability in co-cultured neurons [
55
].
Notably, our work extends beyond neuronal mechanisms by implicating astrocytes as key mediators of BSN-related epileptogenesis. The upregulation of lipid metabolism proteins (APOE, FASN) in BSN-mutant astrocytes suggests a compensatory response to impaired lipid homeostasis. APOE, a lipid transporter critical for cholesterol efflux, is paradoxically linked to neurotoxicity when dysregulated [
56
]. APOE4 isoforms promote lipid droplet accumulation and neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease and epilepsy [
24
,
57
,
58
]. We propose that BSN mutations disrupt APOE-mediated lipid redistribution, leading to astrocytic lipid overload. This metabolic imbalance may impair astrocyte-neuron metabolic coupling, as lipid-laden astrocytes exhibit reduced lactate production, depriving neurons of energy substrates during hyperactivity [
41
].
The observed link between sustained cholesterol accumulation and reduced arginase 1 activity in BSN-mutant astrocytes may reflect a broader disruption of metabolic homeostasis. Arginase deficiency has been shown to induce tissue lipid accumulation via enhanced de novo lipogenesis independent of systemic metabolic changes [
59
]. Moreover, arginase is expressed in activated astrocytes [
60
,
61
], where it can influence nitric oxide production and downstream lipid metabolism. Our findings raise the possibility that BSN mutations impair astrocytic lipid clearance both directly, through altered cholesterol handling, and indirectly, through reduced arginase 1 activity.
Although Bassoon is classically defined as a presynaptic scaffolding protein, our transcriptomic analyses confirm its expression in astrocytes. The persistent cholesterol accumulation observed in BSN-mutant astrocytes resembles metabolic phenotypes of arginase deficiency, where impaired arginase signaling promotes lipid buildup [
59
]. Given that astrocytes are the main source of brain cholesterol and its imbalance contributes to epilepsy [
24
,
62
], our findings highlight a potential non-canonical role of Bassoon in glial cholesterol–arginase regulation.
Our co-culture experiments demonstrated elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α) and reactive oxygen species (ROS) in neurons exposed to BSN-mutant astrocytes. These findings are consistent with emerging evidence that lipid peroxidation products, such as 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), activate the TLR4/MyD88/ERK pathways in astrocytes, thereby triggering pro-inflammatory cascades [
63
]. Moreover, the hyperphosphorylation of ERK and CREB observed in our mutant astrocytes further substantiates this paradigm, as ERK signaling amplifies inflammatory responses and disrupts glutamate uptake by downregulating excitatory amino acid transporters 1 and 2 (EAAT1/2) [
64
]. This creates a vicious cycle: lipid accumulation promotes inflammation, which in turn exacerbates lipid dysregulation and synaptic dysfunction. While our PSD95 staining demonstrates structural synaptic loss in neurons co-cultured with BSN-mutant astrocytes, future studies employing miniature EPSC recordings will be valuable to confirm functional synaptic deficits.
Interestingly, the impaired Kir4.1 channel activity observed in mutant astrocytes may reflect both lipid-induced membrane rigidity and inflammatory pathway activation. Kir4.1 is essential for potassium buffering, and its dysfunction leads to extracellular K
+
accumulation, neuronal depolarization, and seizure susceptibility [
65
,
66
]. Our data suggest that BSN mutations synergistically target ion homeostasis and lipid metabolism, creating a permissive environment for epileptogenesis.
In addition to Kir4.1, we found that TREK-1 expression was also reduced in BSN-mutant astrocytes, pointing toward a broader impairment of astrocytic K
+
channel regulation. Since both Kir4.1 and TREK-1 are essential for maintaining extracellular K
+
levels and modulating neuronal excitability, their downregulation may synergistically contribute to the hyperexcitability observed in BSN-mutant co-cultures. In contrast, BK channels were unaffected, indicating selective vulnerability of inward rectifying and two-pore domain channels to BSN dysfunction.
Given that astrocytes are electrically non-excitable and typically signal through Ca
2+
dynamics [
67
,
68
], our use of RMP reflects ionic dysregulation rather than excitability per se. Future studies incorporating Ca
2+
imaging will be essential to further characterize astrocyte functional responses in the context of BSN mutations.
While elevated extracellular K
+
from impaired Kir4.1 buffering likely contributes to neuronal depolarization and increased firing frequency, the modest elevation of AP amplitude is less straightforward. Astrocyte-derived cholesterol and lipid signals can enhance membrane excitability and support Na
+
channel clustering, potentially counteracting depolarization-induced Na
+
channel inactivation [
69
,
70
]. Additionally, astrocytic secreted factors and gliotransmitters influence intrinsic neuronal excitability [
68
,
71
]. These convergent mechanisms may explain why AP amplitude was preserved or even enhanced in our co-culture system. Future studies with direct Na
+
channel recordings will be essential to clarify these pathways.
The CRISPR/Cas9-edited iPSC model employed here offers unprecedented precision in studying human-specific epilepsy mechanisms [
72
]. By introducing patient-derived mutations into a controlled genetic background, we circumvent the limitations of animal models, which often fail to recapitulate human lipid metabolism pathways. For example, our proteomic analysis revealed APOB upregulation—a feature absents in rodent astrocytes—highlighting the value of human iPSC systems.
Furthermore, the co-culture platform illustrated how astrocyte-specific BSN mutations propagate neuronal injury through non-cell-autonomous mechanisms. This model could be expanded to investigate
trans
-synaptic signaling, including Bassoon-dependent secretion of exosomes or cytokines that modulate astrocyte reactivity. Future studies that integrate lipidomics and metabolomics, such as Seahorse assays for fatty acid oxidation, may reveal additional metabolic vulnerabilities.
Our findings identify lipid metabolism as a potential therapeutic target for BSN-related epilepsy. Agents that modulate APOE, such as the neuroprotective peptide COG1410, may reduce lipid droplet accumulation and neuroinflammation [
56
,
73
]. Similarly, ERK inhibitors, such as Ulixertinib, could disrupt the TLR4/ERK/CREB axis, thereby restoring astrocyte homeostasis. Additionally, repurposing PPARγ agonists, such as pioglitazone, may enhance lipid clearance and glutamate uptake, effectively addressing both metabolic and excitotoxic challenges.
Clinically, patient-derived iPSCs could enable personalized drug screening [
74
]. For example, neurons co-cultured with astrocytes expressing APOE3 versus those expressing APOE4 may demonstrate differential responses to lipid-lowering therapies, thereby informing tailored therapeutic interventions.
While our iPSC model provides critical insights, it cannot fully replicate the complexities of the epileptic brain. The functions of mature astrocytes, such as scar formation and interaction with microglia, necessitate validation in vivo. Utilizing conditional BSN knockout mice or employing xenotransplantation of mutant astrocytes into rodent hippocampi could effectively bridge this gap.
While our isogenic CRISPR model minimizes genetic background noise (validated by karyotyping and off-target screening in
Supplementary Figs. 2–3
), we acknowledge that mechanistic exploration remains incomplete and that validation in patient-derived iPSCs will be essential to establish the full spectrum of BSN dysfunction. Future work will aim to delineate the pathways linking Bassoon's scaffolding role to lipid dysregulation and altered neurotrophic signaling. Notably, the concordance between mutation severity (frameshift ​> ​homozygous missense ​> ​heterozygous) and phenotypic gradation strongly implicates BSN loss-of-function as the primary driver.
The nuclear roles of Bassoon remain largely unexplored. Preliminary evidence suggests that Bassoon may regulate transcription through interactions with chromatin modifiers—this hypothesis could be tested using ChIP-seq or CRISPR interference techniques. Finally, longitudinal studies are essential to ascertain whether lipid-lowering interventions can prevent epileptogenesis or merely alleviate symptoms.
In summary, BSN mutations drive epilepsy through dual mechanisms: disrupting presynaptic integrity and hijacking astrocyte lipid metabolism. Our CRISPR-iPSC platform elucidates how genetic lesions propagate across neural networks, providing a roadmap for targeted therapies. By unraveling the interplay between synaptic proteins and glial metabolism, this work redefines epilepsy as a disorder of cellular symbiosis, paving the way for mechanistically grounded treatments.
